Q: . Mr. Stepanovich -- is it Stepanovich?
A: . Stepanovich.

Q: . Okay. Completely different. Do you understand that you are under oath today?
A: . Yes, I do.

Q: . And this is a formal proceeding but you can ask questions. Do you understand?
A: . Yes.

Q: . If you don't understand what I'm saying at any point, please ask for clarification.
A: . Okay.

Q: . And if you don't know the answer to any question that I'm asking you, please don't guess, just say that you don't know.
A: . Okay.

Q: . If there's a document that might help you recall something, please let me know. And during the course of this deposition if there's something that you want to correct or add to at any point, just let me know. I just ask that you not interrupt -- if I'm talking, that you not interrupt me. We shouldn't interrupt each other because the court reporter can't accurately record that.
A: . Okay.

Q: . But I guess you can wait until I'm finished with what I'm saying and then just let me know if there's something you have to say. The court reporter can't hear us when we're making any nonverbal gestures, so if you nod your head, she won't catch that, so I might ask that you verbalize whatever you were signaling. Is that okay?
A: . That's fine.

Q: . And, again, she can't transcribe what we're saying if we're talking over each other, so I'd ask that you wait until I finish and I'll do the same for you. Okay? If you need a break at any point, that's understandable. Please just let me know. But the only exception is if we're in the middle of a question and you haven't answered yet, so after you finish your answer is fine, but you can take break at any point. All right?
A: . Okay.

Q: . Are you under the -- have you taken any medication that could interfere with your ability to testify today?
A: . No.

Q: . And were there any alcoholic beverages you took this morning?
A: . No.

Q: . Okay. Any other reason you can't testify truthfully today?
A: . No.

Q: . Thank you. Okay. Can you say and spell your name one more time for the court reporter?
A: . Jeff Stepanovich. J-E-F-F, S-T-E-P-A-N-O-V-I-C-H.

Q: . So your name is Jeff and not Jeffrey?
A: . My formal name is Jeffrey. Jeffrey John, yes.

Q: . Okay. Can you spell Jeffrey for me.
A: . J-E-F-F-R-E-Y.

Q: . Okay. Thank you. And have you ever been deposed before?
A: . No.

Q: . Did you prepare for today's deposition?
A: . Prepare as in?

Q: . Did you review any documents in preparation for today's deposition?
A: . I went -- MR. STORCH: Object to the extent that the question calls for attorney/client privilege. So don't discuss anything that you discussed with me or anyone in my office or any documents that we exchanged such as emails. BY MS. WASHINGTON:

Q: . Okay. Yeah. And he's correct. You shouldn't reveal -- I'm not asking you to reveal any conversations that you had with your attorney, but if there were any documents that you reviewed to prepare you for today?
A: . No.

Q: . Okay. And did you meet with your lawyer to prepare for this deposition?
A: . No.

Q: . Okay. Do you -- and we'll kind of shift gears a little bit. So what's your current address?
A: . 1100 Holiday Lane, Naples, Florida 34104.

Q: . And do you own that?
A: . Yes.

Q: . How long have you owned it?
A: . Roughly five years.

Q: . Okay. Where did you live before that?
A: . 10651 Regent Circle, Naples, Florida.

Q: . Did you own that?
A: . Yes.

Q: . How long did you live there?
A: . Seventeen years.

Q: . And what is your current phone number?
A: . Cell phone? (239) 206-9855.

Q: . What's the cell phone provider?
A: . Sprint.

Q: . And how long have you had that number?
A: . I don't know, roughly, 10 years probably.

Q: . Are you currently married?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And what's your wife's name?
A: . Lora, L-O-R-A.

Q: . L-O-R-A. Stepanovich?
A: . Yes.

Q: . How long have you been married?
A: . Twenty-seven years.

Q: . And does Lora live with you?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Has she lived with you at Holiday Lane?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And Regent Circle?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And what's her occupation?
A: . Small business owner.

Q: . What kind of business is it?
A: . She's a concierge for estate homes.

Q: . Estate homes?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. Do you have any children?
A: . Four.

Q: . Are any of them under 18?
A: . No.

Q: . Can you tell me their names and occupations?
A: . Jerry works for Toyota in San Antonio. Garrett works for Shell Oil in Houston and Pittsburg, Pennsylvania. Jessica works for Wright Medical and Madison works for the SBA in St. Pete.

Q: . Does Jessica live in Florida?
A: . Yes. In St. Pete as well.

Q: . And Jerry and Garrett live in Texas?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Do any of them currently live with you?
A: . No.

Q: . Now, are you a member of any social organizations?
A: . No.

Q: . What about professional organizations?
A: . No.

Q: . Let's talk about your education. Tell us about -- did you graduate high school?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Can you tell us about your education since high school?
A: . Bachelor's in education, Western Michigan University, graduated in 1983.

Q: . 1983?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay.
A: . Did my graduate at Western Michigan in 1992.

Q: . So did you get a graduate degree?
A: . No. I'm two classes short.

Q: . And have you attended any trade school?
A: . No.

Q: . Vocational school?
A: . No.

Q: . Do you have any licenses besides a driver's license?
A: . No.

Q: . Any certifications?
A: . No.

Q: . You have a driver's license?
A: . Yes.

Q: . What state?
A: . Florida.

Q: . Have you ever filed for bankruptcy?
A: . No.

Q: . So tell us about your employment since you graduated high school.
A: . Since high school?

Q: . Yes.
A: . Construction while I was in college. I worked for General Motors during the summer for my last two years in college. Once I graduated from college, I was a substitute teacher in Alaska and then I became a legislative aide in Alaska and then I went to work for a company called Executone selling telephone systems and nurse call systems.

Q: . You said Executone?
A: . Executone. Yes.

Q: . Okay.
A: . Upon leaving Alaska and coming to Florida, opened an office for Executone in South Florida, then left them and went with a startup company called Fluid Sense. When I left Fluid Sense, I got in the produce business and went to work for Florida Specialties.

Q: . Can you spell Fluid Sense for me.
A: . F-L-U-I-D S-E-N-S-E. They're no longer in -- S-E-N-S-E, yeah, I think that's what it was.

Q: . They're not in business anymore?
A: . No.

Q: . What did they -- what did you do for them?
A: . We manufactured an infusion pump and I was the vice president of sales from Mississippi east.

Q: . So you did sales there?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. What is an infusion pump?
A: . What you get hooked up to when you get your fluids in the hospital.

Q: . Okay. So medical equipment?
A: . Yes.

Q: . All right. So we'll come back to the produce business -- when you got -- when you went to the produce business.
A: . Okay.

Q: . Florida Specialties. But I just wanted to fill in some of the -- ask you some more questions about the other jobs that you held. So for Executone, what did you do there?
A: . I sold telephone systems and nurse call equipment.

Q: . Nurse call equipment?
A: . Yes.

Q: . That's used in a hospital?
A: . When you lay in bed and call your nurse. Yes.

Q: . Okay. And you said that you moved from Alaska to Florida and opened an office in Florida for Executone?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Was it -- were you doing the same thing?
A: . Yes.

Q: . When you said you opened the office, did you manage it?
A: . I was the southern sales manager. Yes.

Q: . Were you in management in -- before you moved to Florida?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. So I guess we can -- why -- so why did you leave Executone and move into the produce business? Excuse me. Why did you leave Executone and move to Fluid Sense?
A: . Fluid Sense was a financial opportunity to own part of the company and be the vice president of the eastern region.

Q: . Okay. And eastern region, did that encompass a certain number of states?
A: . The Mississippi River east.

Q: . So would that be -- that would encompass Florida and Georgia?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Any other states?
A: . Yes. South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, DC, Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Kentucky, Illinois. What am I missing? Iowa, Tennessee. Without a map in front of me, I think I got most of them.

Q: . So half the country pretty much?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. East of the Mississippi River?
A: . Correct.

Q: . Okay. So when you said that you were the vice president, what did that -- I mean, what were your duties in that position?
A: . Basically responsible for sales and implementation of a new infusion pump throughout the eastern seaboard of the United States.

Q: . And when you were at Fluid Sense, do you -- what was your -- what were you compensated there? What was your compensation?
A: . Salary and then commission.

Q: . And could you tell me the years that you were at Fluid Sense?
A: . Without notes in front of me, I can't give you the exact dates, no.

Q: . Okay. Do you remember generally what your salary and commission, what the total was maybe the last year you were there?
A: . Upper 100 -- upper lower -- it was probably 180 to $200,000.

Q: . All right. So tell us how you started in the produce business with Florida Specialties. How did you make that transition from Fluid Sense?
A: . Our product at Fluid Sense was regulated by the FDA. We manufactured it outside of Boston. We had a self-reported seal failure on one piece of equipment and the FDA shut us down, so the company went into bankruptcy.

Q: . And at that point when the company went into bankruptcy, what did you do?
A: . I was coaching a girls' softball team and one of my players' father was a farmer and he gave me the opportunity to go in the produce business.

Q: . And how did he do that?
A: . He asked me if I wanted a job.

Q: . Did he work for Florida Specialties?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. He was a farmer that supplied product to Florida Specialties?
A: . He was a grower for Florida Specialties and a nephew of the owner of the company.

Q: . And what was his name?
A: . Skeeter Bethea.

Q: . How do you spell Bethea?
A: . B-E-T-H-E-A.

Q: . And who was the owner of the company?
A: . Jim Joiner.

Q: . And where were you living at that time?
A: . In Naples.

Q: . Have you continuously been in Naples since that point until now?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. So tell me about how you -- after your conversation with Mr. Bethea or after your opportunity -- how did your opportunity come about after that introduction?
A: . Skeeter knew I was going to need a job. He offered me an opportunity to talk with his uncle, Jim Joiner. I met with Mr. Joiner; he offered me a job.

Q: . And do you remember when you started that job?
A: . September 9th, 2001. I believe that's the date.

Q: . And what was the position you were hired for?
A: . Sales.

Q: . Was your position salesman?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. And what was your compensation there?
A: . That would be a guess. It was, I think, 65 or 75,000 plus commission.

Q: . Okay. And do you remember what you made that first year? I guess you would have been employed there between September and December. Do you remember what you made that first year?
A: . No, I don't.

Q: . The commission, what was that based on?
A: . It was a 5-3-1, so based on who we sold. We got a commission. Either a 5 percent, 3 percent or 1 percent.

Q: . Okay. So you were at -- just to recap, you started at Florida Specialties as a salesman on September 9th, 2001. And did you have any jobs between Florida Specialties and Ken Corbett Farms? Were there any other jobs?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. What was that?
A: . I worked for Pacific Collier. Pacific Collier.

Q: . Okay. Can you spell Collier for me?
A: . C-O-L-L-I-E-R.

Q: . Okay. Pacific Collier. What did you do there?
A: . I was the director of marketing.

Q: . When was that?
A: . It was 2002, is when I started there.

Q: . And did you work there and Florida Specialties?
A: . No. I left Florida Specialties to go to work for Pacific Collier.

Q: . Okay. Do you remember what month in 2002?
A: . Sometime that summer.

Q: . So you worked for Florida Specialties for less than a year?
A: . Correct.

Q: . And then -- well, how long were you at Pacific Collier?
A: . Roughly four years.

Q: . So from 2004 to 2006?
A: . Roughly, yes.

Q: . And what was your compensation there?
A: . It was over 100,000. I just don't remember what it was.

Q: . And why did you leave Florida Specialties to go there?
A: . Florida Specialties didn't have any benefit package or anything, and I had four young kids. So -- no insurance. So Pacific Collier offered all of those things.

Q: . So why did you leave Pacific Collier?
A: . They shut down their farming operations.

Q: . So they were -- what was the line of business -- what kind of business was Pacific Collier in?
A: . Produce business.

Q: . Okay. So there was marketing for produce?
A: . Marketing and selling for produce. Yes.

Q: . So when you left Pacific Collier, where did you go after that?
A: . Went back to Florida Specialties.

Q: . And that was in 2006?
A: . Roughly. Yes.

Q: . And was Mr. --
A: . Joiner.

Q: . -- Jim Joiner still the owner?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. So did you approach him about a job?
A: . He called me.

Q: . Okay. Did he know that you were not working at Pacific Collier anymore?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And did you -- I'm sorry if I asked you this before, but did you -- you said that Pacific Collier got out of the produce business. So did you -- were you terminated -- were you fired or did you resign?
A: . They were down-staffing, so ...

Q: . You were laid off?
A: . I was laid off, I guess.

Q: . And Mr. Joiner knew that you were laid off and contacted you?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. And you accepted a job?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Do you remember when you started there again?
A: . Probably that fall.

Q: . Fall of 2006?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. Did you have any other jobs between when you started back at Florida Specialties and they -- did you have any jobs between Florida Specialties when you started back in 2006 and Ken Corbett Farms?
A: . Ask me that another -- again, please.

Q: . Were there any other jobs between -- were there any other jobs -- where did you go after you came back to -- tell me how -- hold on. Let me get my thoughts together. When did you start working for Ken Corbett Farms? What year was that?
A: . Directly for him?

Q: . Yes.
A: . Or selling for him?

Q: . Directly for him as an employee.
A: . What was it, 2011?

Q: . Okay. So were there any other jobs -- did you work anywhere else besides Florida Specialties before 2011?
A: . No.

Q: . Okay. So now we can -- when you went back to Florida Specialties in 2006, did you do the same job that you did when you were there before?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. Was it the same compensation?
A: . No.

Q: . How was the compensation different this time?
A: . I negotiated a larger salary and had some other responsibilities added.

Q: . And what were those?
A: . I built their food safety program. I was also responsible for purchasing all of the box material, so ...

Q: . So how much was that salary?
A: . It was over a hundred and something thousand.

Q: . And was there still a commission component?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And what was that?
A: . It varied.

Q: . Okay. Was that the same 5-3-1 you were --
A: . No.

Q: . Can you explain what it was?
A: . It was just -- if I remember correctly, just a straight commission. There wasn't an adjustable.

Q: . Okay. Now, you testified earlier that -- you asked me a question about when you started selling for Ken Corbett Farms. Do you remember that? You asked me when.
A: . Yes.

Q: . So I guess it will be a good time to transition into how you started selling for Ken Corbett Farms. So tell us about that.
A: . Selling for them, not working for them; correct?

Q: . Correct. Correct. When was that?
A: . It was, I believe, two years before I went to work for him.

Q: . So 2009?
A: . Roughly, I guess. Yeah, somewhere around there.

Q: . Okay. So tell us how you started selling for him in 2009.
A: . Ken and his son Justin came to Florida Specialties, we met and talked about what they were trying to do, and I discussed it with Mr. Joiner. He wanted to be an agent for Corbett Farms.

Q: . When you say -- tell me, what city is Florida Specialties located in.
A: . Immokalee.

Q: . I-M-O-K-L --
A: . I-M-M-O-K-A-L-E-E.

Q: . I-M-M-O-K-A-L-E-E. Okay. So when you say that Ken Corbett came to Florida Specialties, what does that mean?
A: . Him and his son showed up one day. I believe they were in Immokalee looking for a new sales agent to handle their product and they came to our facility, and I was the one who met with them.

Q: . Okay. Can you tell us the details about that first conversation.
A: . I don't really recall any specific details, no.

Q: . And when you say "his son," who are you referring to?
A: . His son Justin.

Q: . Okay. Justin Corbett?
A: . Yes.

Q: . So they showed up in person --
A: . Correct.

Q: . -- to the -- okay. And you spoke with them?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And you testified earlier that Ken Corbett wanted Florida Specialties to be an agent for them?
A: . Was looking for someone to sell his product, yes.

Q: . Okay. And this is produce?
A: . Correct.

Q: . And you had a conversation with the owner about this?
A: . After, yes.

Q: . And the owner agreed?
A: . Correct.

Q: . Now, what was the -- what was that arrangement? Can you tell us about that?
A: . If I remember correctly, it was pretty much a standard. We got 6 percent commission, I believe, on the product that we sold of Ken's.

Q: . Okay. So you were paid 6 percent commission off the product that was sold?
A: . I was not paid 6 percent, no.

Q: . Who was paid?
A: . Florida Specialties was paid 6 percent.

Q: . And that agreement, was it in writing?
A: . I believe so.

Q: . And when you say that you sold the product, was that you personally sold the product?
A: . It was myself and Chris Tortinato in our sales office sold the product.

Q: . Tortinato?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. And how did you go about selling that product?
A: . Communicating with our existing client base.

Q: . Can you walk me through that process, how you did that.
A: . Generally, on any given day, we would be notified how much product would be produced that day, and then once we found that out, we would start selling it that morning.

Q: . Who would notify you how much product was being produced?
A: . Usually the farmer which was Justin.

Q: . So then you got on the phone and called contacts?
A: . Yes.

Q: . Okay. And when you say existing client base, are those people who you have sold to before?
A: . Sold to before and new, yes.

Q: . And new?
A: . And we would have to develop new customers because Georgia was a different sales window than what we sold in Florida.

Q: . And what does that mean?
A: . Production time period. We didn't sell that particular product in Georgia, we didn't grow it, so having peppers and eggplant, et cetera was a different -- it just was -- we grew green beans in Georgia. Florida Specialties did. We didn't grow vegetables. So we grew vegetables in Florida, but not in Georgia.

Q: . So Florida Specialties, they were farmers and -- so Florida Specialties had its own farmers?
A: . Yes.

Q: . That grew green beans in Florida?
A: . And vegetables, yes.

Q: . Okay. And Ken Corbett grew vegetables in Georgia?
A: . Correct.

Q: . So you at Florida Specialties purchased Mr. Corbett's vegetables and sold them to your clients?
A: . We didn't purchase them. We were a sales agent for Mr. Corbett.

Q: . Okay. So how did you develop new clients, new customers?
A: . Like all sales people. On the phone, at trade shows, those kind of things.

Q: . So when you talk about your client base you refer to people that you've sold to already?
A: . Correct.

Q: . Right? So new clients would not be -- or potential clients would not be included in your client base?
A: . They wouldn't be considered a client yet until I sold them something.

Q: . So how was that -- how long did you sell the product, Ken Corbett's product, while you were employed at Florida Specialties?
A: . I think roughly two years.

Q: . And how profitable was that arrangement?
A: . I don't know.

Q: . And when did you leave Florida Specialties?
A: . 2000 -- let's see. I'm trying to work backwards. 2011, I believe.

Q: . 2011. And why did you leave?
A: . I was let go.

Q: . Were you laid off?
A: . No.

Q: . Can you explain what "let go" means?
A: . New owner, him and I didn't agree on some issues so he fired me.

Q: . What's his name?
A: . Myles Strolh.

Q: . M-I-L-E-S?
A: . M-Y-L-E-S, I believe, S-T-R-O-L-H, I think.

Q: . S-T-R-O-L-H. Okay. And what didn't you agree on?
A: . Mainly building a new processing facility, where it should be located.

Q: . And what happened after you were terminated?

et me know when you're done. Do you recognize that document that we're calling Plaintiff's Response to Defendant's Interrogatories? (Defendant's Exhibit No. 4 was marked for identification.)

Q: . And you had it in June?

Q: . Now, did you have any -- were there any doctor's appointments that you had when you were -- when you underwent the test to determine that you had prostate cancer, did you have any doctor's appointments that you attended?

Q: . Did you -- okay. Did you actually have to visit the doctor's office or any other facility to give samples for the test before you were diagnosed with prostate cancer?
A: . There was a process once the first test came back negative, yes.

Q: . And that process was to take tests?
A: . Correct.

Q: . Right. And about how many of those were there?
A: . There was, I believe, two more PSA -- one more PSA test, and then it came back high and then I went in for a biopsy which is an invasive procedure where they took biopsies that were then sent to the lab.

Q: . Okay.
A: . Took them from -- the cancer was there.

Q: . So there were -- am I counting three appointments?
A: . I would have to check my personal calendar. I would say at least three, yes.

Q: . Before the diagnosis?
A: . Before it was confirmed, yes.

Q: . And after your physical?
A: . Correct.

Q: . Okay. And did you -- was there any push-back from Mr. Corbett in going to these appointments?
A: . There wouldn't have been because I wasn't in Georgia at the time.

Q: . When did you come back to Georgia, what date?
A: . I could look at my calendar, but generally I'd come up for most of the month of October and November.

Q: . So you came -- so in 2016, you were in Georgia in October and November. And when did you come back in 2017?
A: . I did not.

Q: . Oh, so you didn't come back to Georgia at all in 2017?
A: . No. He released me before I was -- I was getting ready to come back up. We had started production in squash, so ...

Q: . Now, what was your recovery time for your surgery?
A: . A little over six weeks.

Q: . And was there -- and we'll talk about this in more detail later but was -- when you were terminated from Ken Corbett Farms, what was the first -- well, did you start searching for a job immediately?
A: . I'm sure I started having conversations with people, yes, letting them know I was available.

Q: . And when did you start the first job after you left Ken Corbett Farms?
A: . That was with Windsor Distributing, and I don't know the exact date. I think it was --

Q: . Go ahead. I'm sorry.
A: . I just don't remember the exact day, so ...

Q: . Was it after your recovery from surgery?
A: . Yes.

Q: . And you drew Unemployment at some point during 2017; right?
A: . Right.

Q: . And was that after your recovery period?
A: . I would have to look at the dates.

Q: . Oh, this has nothing to do with United States. Okay. So where do these other packages come from in the total packages category?
A: . I guess they could have just been in as cash or they could have been in as samples or they could have been in as some other items, so ...

Q: . Were they not calculated for purposes of that percentage?
A: . It didn't matter. It wasn't enough of them. It was just a number.

Q: . Okay. So I see below Eric's name for 2011 there's $2,336,925 and under "total us" it's $10,802,696. So isn't that the same -- those are the same calculations, but for the actual money that you brought in?
A: . Correct.

Q: . So the percentages, for example, for Eric of 22 percent, he brought in 22 percent of your total sales?
A: . Of revenue, yeah.

Q: . Of revenue. In 2011.
A: . Again, these are rough numbers. That's all they were.

Q: . And what do you mean by rough numbers?
A: . I mean, I just ran a quick report based on salesman and product. I'm sure that's what I ran. So I didn't verify anything, I didn't see if anything changed later. These were just numbers on the day I ran them.

Q: . Okay. So it was subject to -- those numbers were subject to being changed at a later date?

A: . Yes.

A: . They were for us to discuss, yes.

Q: . You only recall you doing it?
